title: Regression in practice & causality
source: Session 10 handout (DDM 26/27) – Antonakis et al. (2010), Airbnb New York/Melbourne, grocery shopping, movie box office; Playmobil (exam 2019/20) and H&M (revision session)
tagline: A regression coefficient is only a causal effect if the independent variable is exogenous. Otherwise – reverse causality, omitted variables – it is an association. You may predict with associations, but you should only give policy recommendations based on causal effects.
goals: state the **three conditions** for a causal claim
explain **reverse causality, omitted variables** and **spurious correlations**
say when a coefficient may be read **causally** (exogenous x)
build and interpret a model with **dummy variables** and make a **prediction**
turn a coefficient table into **managerial recommendations** and name its limitations

items: Intercept: the **estimated** value of the DV when all IVs equal zero (not the observed one)
Significant coefficient (p < 0.05): when x rises by one unit, y is expected to change by b units, all else equal
Not significant (p ≥ 0.05): **no change expected** – don't interpret the size, even if it looks large
R²: share of the variance of y explained by the model

blocks.title: Recap quiz pattern
blocks.text: “When social desirability is higher by one unit, how does perceived stress change?” – if the coefficient is **insignificant**, the correct answer is “we do not expect any change”, not “lower by 0.149”.

blocks.title: x → y is causal only if … (Antonakis et al., 2010)

steps.label: Reliable correlation
steps.text: x must be correlated with y **beyond chance**

steps.label: No alternative explanation
steps.text: The relation must **not** be explained by other causes

blocks.text: If x is (potentially) **endogenous**, the regression coefficient must be interpreted as an **association** (correlational). Two major reasons:

items.caption: **Reverse causality / simultaneity**: y also drives x – firms spend more on ads when they expect high sales.
**Omitted variable**: a third variable drives both x and y – the correlation is spurious.
**Exogenous x** (manipulated by an external force, e.g. an experiment or A/B test) → the coefficient is a causal effect.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.text: Causal effects let you **explain past events** and give **appropriate policy recommendations**. Spurious correlations (tylervigen.com) can be highly significant – significance is not causality. Recommendations like “spend more on X” require a causal effect.

items.label: Airbnb New York
items.text: Which factors are associated with price? Room type, number of beds, people accommodated, bathrooms, acceptance rate, review score. Take-home: compare with **Melbourne** – different market, different coefficients.

items.label: Grocery shopping
items.text: Total grocery spending explained by demographics and behaviour; categorical variables (gender, loyalty membership, region) recoded as **dummies**.

items.label: Movie box office
items.text: Predict revenue of “1917” (budget 100 m, 118 min, IMDb 8.37; actual 365.2 m): budget only → + runtime → + rating – each step gets closer to the real value.

blocks.title: Dummy coding
items: A nominal variable with **k categories** becomes **k − 1** dummies (0/1); the left-out category is the **baseline**
The dummy coefficient = difference in y **relative to the baseline**, all else equal (female = 1: women spend b more than men)
Including all k dummies plus an intercept makes the model unidentifiable (dummy-variable trap)

blocks.title: Grocery spending – refined model (practice coefficients)
given: Spending = 120 + 3.5 × age + 45 × female + 22 × visits per year + 180 × loyalty member
Customer: 45 years, female, 37 visits per year, loyalty member
blocks.question: Predicted yearly grocery spending?

steps.label: Hypothesise
steps.text: Which variables should matter and why?

steps.label: Estimate
steps.text: Full model: significance, fit, interpretation, face validity

steps.label: Refine & predict
steps.text: Subset model → prediction for a given customer

blocks.title: Answer scheme for “Which elements have the strongest impact – what do you recommend?”

steps.label: 1 · Significance
steps.text: Keep only p < 0.05 – ignore the rest

steps.label: 2 · Size & sign
steps.text: Rank the significant betas; note negative effects

steps.label: 3 · Recommend
steps.text: Advertising: the significant channel with the largest beta; product: follow significant product effects

steps.label: 4 · Limitations
steps.text: Units, standardisation, R², omitted variables, causality

blocks.title: Playmobil Christmas edition (exam 2019/20): significant betas only
blocks.caption: Not significant: online_spend (0.18) and box age. Strongest elements: outlets (+) and box size (−). Advertise via **billboards**, then TV; prioritise **smaller box sets**; no statement on age suitability.

blocks.title: H&M 2022 forecast (revision session): significant betas
blocks.caption: All three channels are significant – online has by far the largest beta → invest online. The negative coefficient on past sales indicates a **declining** sales trend; new_products is not significant.

items.label: Units & standardisation
items.text: Units of DV and IVs unclear, coefficients not standardised → sizes hard to compare

items.label: Fit not reported
items.text: No R² / adjusted R² → unknown how much is explained

items.label: Omitted variables
items.text: Price, competitors, seasonality, product theme missing

items.label: Reverse causality
items.text: Outlets and ad budgets may follow expected sales

items.label: Fix
items.text: Add controls, more granular data, or run **experiments** for causal effects

recap: Causal claim needs: x before y, reliable correlation, no alternative explanation.
Endogenous x → coefficient is an **association**: reverse causality (y → x) or omitted variables (z → x and y).
Exogenous x (experiment, external manipulation) → **causal** effect; only causal effects justify policy recommendations.
k categories → **k − 1 dummies**; dummy coefficient = difference to the baseline.
Prediction = intercept + Σ (significant coefficient × value) for the described customer.
Recommendation scheme: significance → size/sign → action → limitations.
exam: Coefficient table with significance levels (Playmobil, H&M): strongest elements, advertising and product recommendation, sales trend.
Explain why a coefficient may not be causal and what this means for recommendations.
Limitations of a given model and how to improve it.
traps: Highly significant ≠ causal – spurious correlations can be very significant.
Don't recommend investing in a channel whose coefficient is **not** significant, however large it looks.
A negative coefficient on past sales signals a downward trend, not an error.
Comparing raw betas across variables in different units is misleading without standardisation.
